chunks: Ground layout schemes. The question: What are some ground layout schemes?
A ground layout scheme is the way you wire ground on a board.
In single-point grounding, every circuit returns to one common point, either in a chain or in a star with a separate path for each circuit.
In multipoint grounding, a solid ground plane lets every circuit connect to ground at the nearest spot. Most modern boards use a plane with careful placement.
Think of drainage in a neighborhood. In a chain, all the houses empty into one shared pipe, so the last house feels everyone else's flow.
In a star, each house has its own pipe to the treatment plant, so none affects another.
In a plane, the whole neighborhood sits on a tiled floor with drains everywhere, so water leaves right where it lands.
The analogy is loose: for fast signals a star's long pipes resist sudden changes (inductance), and the plane wins.
In a daisy-chain ground, the return current of the noisy Load B flows through R g2 and then R g1.
The sensitive Load A shares R g1, so its ground reference moves by (I A + I B)·R g1 every time B changes current.
Common-impedance coupling: a shared ground segment turns one circuit's current into noise for another ("What PCB grounding is and why it matters").
Inductance: resistance to changing current. It matters more the faster the current changes. Impedance: resistance and inductance together, in ohms, at a given frequency.
Star ground: each circuit has its own return to a common point ("Star grounding"). ADC and LSB: a chip that turns a voltage into a number, and its smallest step.
Take a 50 mm ground trace, 0. 25 mm wide in standard copper.
Its resistance is about 98 milliohms and its inductance about 60 nanohenries, so above roughly 250 kilohertz the inductance dominates. At 1 megahertz its impedance is about 0.
39 ohms. A 10 milliamps return current then shifts the ground by about 4 millivolts. A 12-bit, 3. 3 volts ADC has steps of 0. 8 millivolts, so that is an error of about 5 steps.
One square of plane is only about 1. 6 milliohms at 1 megahertz, so the same current gives about 0. 02 millivolts. That is the whole idea.
"The main ground layout schemes are single-point, which can be series daisy-chain or parallel star, multipoint, which is a solid ground plane, and hybrids.
Star grounding keeps circuits from sharing return impedance and suits low-frequency analog. A plane gives the lowest inductance and is the right answer for fast digital.
In practice I use a solid plane, partition the board so noisy and quiet circuits don't share return paths, and join sections at one controlled point."
Quick check. Which scheme gives each circuit its own dedicated return path to one common point?
